title: Ownership & How Title Is Held
originality: All items original to LicensePath. Modeled on the DRE exam blueprint and style only; no actual exam items reproduced.

questions.stem: Ownership in severalty means the property is owned by:
options: Several persons in equal shares
One person or entity alone
Two or more persons with right of survivorship
A married couple as community property
rationales: The word suggests multiple owners, which is precisely the trap; severalty is sole ownership.
Correct. Severalty is ownership by one person or one entity, with the interest severed from all others.
That describes joint tenancy.
Community property is a form of concurrent ownership between spouses.

questions.stem: The four unities required for a valid joint tenancy are:
options: Time, title, interest, and possession
Time, transfer, intent, and payment
Title, taxes, interest, and possession
Time, title, inheritance, and partition
rationales: Correct. T-TIP: all joint tenants take at the same time, by the same title, in equal interests, with equal right of possession.
Transfer, intent, and payment are not unities.
Taxes is not a unity.
Inheritance and partition are consequences of ownership form, not unities.

questions.stem: Two sisters own a home as joint tenants. One dies leaving a will devising 'all my real property' to her son. The son receives:
options: A one-half interest as a tenant in common
A one-half interest as a joint tenant
Nothing from this property
The entire property, subject to the sister's life estate
rationales: The decedent's interest never entered her estate, so nothing passed to be held in common.
Survivorship does not admit new joint tenants by will.
Correct. In joint tenancy the interest passes automatically to the surviving joint tenant at death; a will cannot defeat the right of survivorship.
No life estate exists; the surviving sister owns the whole in severalty.

questions.stem: Three friends hold title as joint tenants, each owning one-third. One sells her interest to an outsider. Immediately after the sale:
options: All three owners are tenants in common
The outsider is a joint tenant with the other two
The two remaining friends are joint tenants as to two-thirds; the outsider holds one-third as a tenant in common
The sale is void without the other joint tenants' consent
rationales: The severance affects only the transferred interest; the remaining joint tenancy survives.
The outsider took at a different time by a different deed, breaking unities of time and title.
Correct. Severance converts only the conveyed share to a tenancy in common, while the untouched interests remain in joint tenancy with survivorship.
A joint tenant may convey her interest without the others' consent.

questions.stem: When two unmarried people take title and the deed does not specify how, California presumes they hold as:
options: Joint tenants
Tenants in common
Partners
Owners in severalty
rationales: Joint tenancy must be expressly stated in the deed; it is never presumed.
Correct. Tenancy in common is California's default form of concurrent ownership when the deed is silent.
A partnership requires a partnership relationship, not merely co-ownership.
Severalty is sole ownership, impossible with two grantees.

questions.stem: Which characteristic belongs to tenancy in common but NOT to joint tenancy?
options: Unity of possession
The right to sell one's interest without the others' consent
Ownership shares that may be unequal
The right to seek partition
rationales: Both forms require unity of possession.
Both joint tenants and tenants in common may convey their interests without consent.
Correct. Joint tenancy requires equal interests (unity of interest); tenancy in common permits unequal shares such as 60/25/15.
Co-owners under either form may bring a partition action.

questions.stem: Property acquired by one spouse during marriage by inheritance from a parent is presumed to be:
options: Community property
Separate property
Community property with right of survivorship
Joint tenancy property
rationales: The community presumption covers property acquired through the labor or earnings of either spouse, not gifts and inheritances.
Correct. Property acquired during marriage by gift or inheritance is separate property, as is property owned before marriage or bought with separate funds.
That is a vesting choice, not a presumption arising from inheritance.
Joint tenancy requires an express deed statement.

questions.stem: A married couple holds their residence as community property. The husband alone signs a deed selling the home. The conveyance is:
options: Valid, because each spouse owns an undivided one-half
Defective, because both spouses must join in a conveyance of community real property
Valid if the wife is notified within 30 days
Valid as to the husband's half only, creating a tenancy in common with the buyer
rationales: The undivided one-half interest does not authorize a unilateral sale of the whole.
Correct. Both spouses must join in a conveyance or encumbrance of community real property; a missing spousal signature will stop the closing.
No notice provision cures the missing signature.
California law does not treat the attempted conveyance as an effective half-transfer creating co-ownership with a stranger.

questions.stem: Four cousins own land as joint tenants, each one-quarter. Cousin A deeds her interest to a friend. Cousin B then dies with a will leaving everything to his son. Ownership is now:
options: Friend 1/4; C 3/8; D 3/8
Friend 1/4; son 1/4; C 1/4; D 1/4
Friend 1/4; son 1/4; C 3/8; D 1/8
rationales: Correct. A's conveyance severs 1/4 to the friend as a tenant in common; B, C, and D hold 3/4 in joint tenancy, so B's death passes his share to C and D, giving each 3/8.
The son takes nothing — survivorship within the surviving joint tenancy defeats the will.
The son has no interest, and C and D share B's interest equally.
The friend's severed one-quarter interest remains intact.

questions.stem: Three tenants in common — 50%, 30%, and 20% — sell for $690,000 with 7% total costs and a $310,000 loan payoff. The 30% owner nets:
rationales: $207,000 is 30% of the gross price, ignoring costs and the loan payoff.
$114,210 applies the 30% share after costs but before the loan payoff.
$165,850 is the 50% owner's share.

questions.stem: Co-owners deadlock: two want to sell, one refuses. The legal remedy available to any co-owner is:
options: A quiet title action
A partition action
An unlawful detainer action
A reformation action
rationales: Quiet title resolves competing claims to title, which are not disputed here.
Correct. A partition action asks the court to divide the property in kind or, more commonly for a single home, order it sold and divide the proceeds.
Unlawful detainer recovers possession from a tenant.
Reformation corrects a document that misstates the parties' agreement.

questions.stem: Title is vested in 'Maria Chen, Trustee of the Chen Family Trust dated March 3, 2015.' To sell, escrow will typically require:
options: The complete trust instrument recorded in the county
A certification of trust evidencing the trustee's authority
Signatures from all trust beneficiaries
A court order approving the sale
rationales: Recording the entire trust would expose private terms unnecessarily and is not the standard practice.
Correct. A certification of trust establishes the trustee's authority to act while keeping the trust's private provisions confidential.
Beneficiaries do not sign; the trustee holds title and conveys.
Court approval is required for some probate and conservatorship sales, not routine living-trust sales.

questions.stem: A corporation with 500 shareholders owns an office building. The corporation holds title:
options: In severalty
As a tenant in common with its shareholders
In joint tenancy with its officers
As community property
rationales: Correct. A corporation is a single legal person, so it owns in severalty no matter how many shareholders it has.
Shareholders own stock, not an interest in the corporation's real property.
Officers hold no title by virtue of office.
Community property applies to spouses, not corporations.

questions.stem: In California, a joint tenant obtains a loan secured by a deed of trust against the property. This act, by itself:
options: Severs the joint tenancy immediately
Does not sever the joint tenancy, because California follows lien theory
Converts all owners to tenants in common
Requires all joint tenants to sign or the loan is void
rationales: Severance requires breaking a unity; a lien does not transfer title.
Correct. In a lien-theory state like California the lender takes a lien rather than title, so recording a deed of trust does not by itself sever a joint tenancy.
No conversion of the other owners' interests occurs.
The lender will want all owners to sign for its own protection, but the encumbrance of one joint tenant's interest is not void without them.

questions.stem: To clear a deceased joint tenant from title, the surviving joint tenant typically records:
options: A quitclaim deed from the decedent's heirs
An affidavit of death of joint tenant with a certified death certificate
A grant deed from the executor
A notice of default
rationales: Heirs have no interest to quitclaim, since survivorship already operated.
Correct. The affidavit of death of joint tenant, recorded with a certified death certificate, evidences that title vested in the survivor by operation of law.
No executor's deed is needed because the interest never entered probate.
A notice of default begins foreclosure and is unrelated.
terms: affidavit of death of joint tenant

questions.stem: A resident of a stock cooperative owns:
options: Fee title to a unit of airspace plus an undivided interest in common areas
Shares in the corporation plus a proprietary lease
A life estate in the unit
An undivided interest in the entire building as a tenant in common
rationales: That describes a condominium, which is real property.
Correct. In a stock cooperative the corporation owns the building and residents own shares plus a proprietary lease — personal property, which is why co-op financing differs.
No measuring life is involved.
Co-op residents do not hold title as tenants in common.

questions.stem: Two co-owners of a Duarte duplex hold undivided one-half interests as tenants in common. This means each owner:
options: Owns one specific unit outright
Has the right to possess the entire property
May exclude the other from half the building
Must obtain the other's consent to sell his interest
rationales: Co-ownership of an undivided interest does not assign specific physical portions.
Correct. Unity of possession gives every co-owner the right to possess and use the whole property, not a divided piece.
Neither co-owner may exclude the other from any part of the property.
A tenant in common may convey his interest freely without consent.

questions.stem: Buyers ask their agent, 'Should we take title as joint tenants or as community property with right of survivorship?' The agent's BEST response is to:
options: Recommend community property with right of survivorship for its tax advantages
Recommend joint tenancy because it avoids probate
Explain the general characteristics of each and refer them to their attorney or CPA
Instruct escrow to select the vesting that is most common locally
rationales: Recommending a vesting for tax reasons is giving legal and tax advice beyond a licensee's authority.
Both vestings can avoid probate; recommending one is still advising on a legal question.
Correct. A licensee may describe the options generally but must refer the choice to an attorney or CPA, because vesting carries legal, estate, and tax consequences.
Delegating a client's legal decision to escrow based on local habit serves no one and does not cure the advice problem.
terms: community property with right of survivorship
